slides.title: Ray Tracing With Conformal Geometry
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as an application stress test. The conformal model supplies a single geometric language, but the renderer still has to survive repeated pixel-scale work. Ask students to listen for the balance between elegant objects and the cheaper representations used in hot loops.

slides.title: The Rendering Pipeline Is a Sequence of Geometric Questions
slides.notes: Use the pipeline as the lecture map. Each box is a question that becomes more local: which direction does the pixel see, which model might be hit, which region contains the ray, which triangle is closest, and which lighting paths are available from the hit point.

slides.title: Conformal Meaning, Deliberate Storage
slides.notes: Emphasize that this is not a rejection of conformal geometry. The algebra names the objects and the invariants, while the implementation stores the form that answers the repeated query cheaply. That distinction is the central engineering lesson of the chapter.

slides.title: Meshes Keep Surface Geometry Inspectable
slides.notes: Make the mesh checks feel practical rather than bureaucratic. Positive areas, unit normals, and enclosing spheres are the guard rails that prevent visual bugs from masquerading as algebraic mistakes. The numbers also show how a transformed box, a smoothed sphere mesh, and a floor enter the same scene.

slides.title: Camera Rays and Bounding Spheres
slides.notes: Treat the camera as a ray factory. The conformal model can describe lines richly, but closest-hit rendering benefits from an origin, a unit direction, and a parameter interval. Bounding spheres are the first conservative test: a miss proves absence, while a hit merely permits finer work.

slides.title: A Triangle Hit Carries Interpolation Data
slides.notes: Slow down on barycentric coordinates because they are the bridge from intersection to shading. The ray parameter locates the surface point, while the three weights decide whether the point is inside the triangle and how vertex normals or other attributes should be interpolated.

slides.title: BSP Traversal Preserves Answers While Reducing Triangle Tests
slides.notes: The acceleration slide should compare correctness and cost separately. The ray bundle has perfect agreement between naive and BSP traversal, so the geometry is preserved. The payoff is visible in primitive counts: many triangle tests are replaced by cheaper box and node decisions.

slides.title: Shading Spawns New Rays From Local Surface Data
slides.notes: After a hit, the geometric question changes. The renderer no longer asks which surface is first; it asks which lights are visible and which outgoing directions contribute. The interpolated normal, finite shadow segment, reflected ray, and optional refraction rule are all local geometric constructions.

slides.title: Evaluation: Elegance Meets Throughput
slides.notes: Connect the notebook statistics to the source page evaluation. The chapter does not claim that the richest conformal representation is always fastest. Instead, it argues for a disciplined compromise: keep conformal operations where they clarify transformations and object relationships, then specialize inner-loop storage when performance matters.

slides.title: Takeaways for Graphics Software
slides.notes: Close with a software-design habit, not a formula list. Let the algebra state what the geometric object is, let the renderer store what each repeated operation needs, and let executable checks protect the bridge between the two. That habit is reusable beyond this small ray tracer.
